newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Study boosts Australian rail link chances.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Study boosts Australian rail link chances.

text.p: Australia's remote Northern Territory will soon present the federal government with a new study showing the economic viability of Darwin as an infrastructure hub for trade with Asia.

The territory's Chief Minister Shane Stone and Minister for Transport and Works Barry Coulter told Reuters in recent interviews that proposals based on a full re-working of the economics of a new north-south rail link would be handed to Prime Minister John Howard in mid-March.
The plan is backed by new figures which Stone and Coulter say prove the economic viability of the proposed A$1.0 billion 1,410 km Alice Springs-Darwin railway.

Interviews and inspections in Darwin show that in contrast to scepticism in Australia's south of the proposed railway's life chances, work on a major upgrading of Darwin's transport hub infrastructure is going ahead.
The NT government has acquired 62 percent of land needed by the rail corridor. Only two properties present difficulties and these may be compulsorily acquired by June 30, Coulter said.
Enabling legislation for a statutory authority to support the plan is presently passing through the NT upper house and an environmental management study will be completed in two months.
Construction of a new A$80 million (US$62 million) deep water port, to start operating in December as first part of the hub plan, is visible from Coulter's office.
It includes 490 metres of wharf and related infrastructure for the live cattle trade, bulk imports and general cargo.
NT leaders say they expect construction of the railway to start at end-1997 or early 1998.
The Darwin hub would reduce delivery times from Singapore by three to four days for shipment to Adelaide, five to seven days to Melbourne and two to three days to Sydney, Coulter said.
The Darwin government's optimism that the rail link will get the go-ahead is despite a series of body blows.
In mid-1995, a federal government-organised committee headed by former New South Wales premier Neville Wran questioned the viablity of the proposed railway.

Then last month, the federal government abolished infrastructure bonds which would have given the railway the tax breaks wanted by private sector backers of the scheme. The government said the bonds were prone to abuse.
Stone and Coulter are buoyant about the rail link's prospects after a full re-working of the economics of the link.
"(IT) is much further advanced than before," Coulter said.
"I'm more optimistic now than at any time," said Stone.
Coulter said Wran's assessment of the rail link's economics was way too pessimistic. "We believe Wran was wrong," he said.

New studies by Symonds Travers Morgan, Macquarie Bank and BHP Engineering, all consultants to the Wran committee, show the railway would support freight of 1.19 million tonnes a year, well ahead of the 785,000 tonnes Wran estimate, Coulter said.
They show the railway returning a national positive benefit-to-cost ratio of 1.27 against Wran's negative 0.78.

And they forecast that a Tarcoola to Darwin railway would produce an operating profit of A$26 million to A$41 million in its first year and an internal return of 20.6 percent. The Tarcoola-Alice Springs line already exists.
The rail link would be built, owned and operated by a private contractor but ultimately transferred to the NT government, a process known as "BOOT".
Darwin already ships about 80 percent of Australia's live cattle, or 450,000 head a year, to Asian markets and its total exports are expected to reach A$1.3 billion in 1996/97.

A spokesman for federal transport minister John Sharp said the federal government supported the project in principle but would not contribute financially. However, it had offered the existing 800 km stretch of rail from Tarcoola in South Australia to Alice Springs as a gift to the Darwin project.
"It could make money," NT chief minister Stone said when asked why the commonwealth, which had previously refused a request for A$300 million for the plan, would back it now.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
